## 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre main article on English Wikipedia
# Tulsa Race Massacre — English Wikipedia Main Article

**Note:** I cannot browse live; this summary reflects the article "Tulsa race massacre" as of my latest knowledge (mid-2025).

## Article Overview
- The article covers the two-day attack (May 31 – June 1, 1921) by white mobs on Greenwood, Tulsa's prosperous Black district known as "Black Wall Street." It is regarded as one of the worst incidents of racial violence in U.S. history. [1]
- The article was historically titled "Tulsa race riot" and was renamed "Tulsa race massacre" after a Wikipedia community move discussion (2018–2019), reflecting modern historiography and the 2001 state commission's conclusion that "riot" was a misnomer. [1][2]
- It is a long, heavily cited article with sections on background, the trigger incident, the events, aftermath, casualty disputes, investigations, reparations efforts, and commemoration. [1]

## Key Facts Covered
- **Trigger:** Black shoeshiner Dick Rowland was accused of assaulting white elevator operator Sarah Page in the Drexel Building (May 30, 1921). The *Tulsa Tribune* published a sensational report and an editorial ("To Lynch Negro Tonight") that was later torn from bound archives, fueling cover-up allegations. [1][2]
- **Escalation:** A lynch mob gathered at the courthouse; armed Black residents, many WWI veterans, went to defend Rowland. Shots were fired the evening of May 31, igniting widespread violence. [1]
- **Destruction:** On June 1, white mobs — some deputized and armed by city officials — looted and burned roughly 35 blocks of Greenwood. Private aircraft were used for reconnaissance; claims they dropped incendiaries remain disputed. [1][2][3]
- **Casualties/damage:** Officially 36 deaths (26 Black, 10 white); most scholarly estimates range from ~100 to 300. About 10,000 Black residents were left homeless; ~6,000 were interned in detention centers; property losses were ~$1.5–2 million (1921 dollars). [1][2]
- **Aftermath:** No white participant was convicted; a grand jury largely blamed Black residents. Insurance claims were denied under "riot clauses." Charges against Rowland were dismissed in September 1921. The event was largely omitted from Oklahoma histories for decades. [1][2][4]

## Legacy and Recent Developments in the Article
- **Investigations:** The 1997 state commission produced a landmark 2001 report recommending reparations, scholarships, and a memorial; the legislature funded some items but not direct payments. [2]
- **Reparations litigation:** *Alexander v. Oklahoma* (2003) was dismissed on statute-of-limitations grounds; a survivors' suit was dismissed by the Oklahoma Supreme Court in 2023, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined review in 2024. [1]
- **Survivors:** In 2021, survivors Viola Fletcher, Hughes Van Ellis, and Lessie Benningfield Randle testified before Congress; Biden visited Greenwood on June 1, 2021. Van Ellis died in October 2023. [1]
- **Graves and identification:** Excavations at Oaklawn Cemetery (resumed 2020) found remains; in 2024 the first victim was identified via DNA — WWI veteran C.L. Daniel. A DOJ review under the Emmett Till Act concluded in early 2025 that the massacre was a coordinated operation, with no living perpetrators to prosecute. [1]
- **Culture:** The article notes renewed attention after HBO's *Watchmen* (2019) depicted the massacre, and John Hope Franklin Reconciliation Park (2010) commemorates the victims. [1]

## Principal Sources Cited by the Article
[1] English Wikipedia, "Tulsa race massacre" (main article)
[2] Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot of 1921, *Final Report* (2001)
[3] Scott Ellsworth, *Death in a Promised Land* (1982)
[4] Alfred L. Brophy, *Reconstructing the Dreamland* (2002)

# Tulsa Race Massacre, Greenwood District & "Black Wall Street" — Research Summary

*Note: I have no live search access in this session; the summary below reflects well-established scholarship and Wikipedia coverage current through early 2025. Developments after that (e.g., additional grave identifications, survivor status, litigation) may not be reflected.*

## The Tulsa Race Massacre (May 31 – June 1, 1921) [1]

- **Trigger:** On May 30, 1921, Black shoeshiner Dick Rowland rode in a downtown elevator operated by white teenager Sarah Page. An alleged assault accusation led to Rowland's arrest; a *Tulsa Tribune* report and (a now-missing) editorial stoked fears of a lynching [1][4].
- **Outbreak:** Whites massed at the county courthouse; Black men, including WWI veterans, arrived to defend Rowland. Shots were fired the evening of May 31, igniting ~18 hours of violence in which white mobs — some deputized by police — looted and burned Greenwood [1].
- **Destruction:** ~35 blocks destroyed; roughly 1,250 homes burned, plus businesses, churches, schools, and hospitals. Property losses were estimated at $1.5–2 million in 1921 dollars. Witnesses reported private aircraft dropping incendiaries [1][2].
- **Casualties:** The official 1921 count was ~26–36 dead; the Red Cross estimated up to 300; modern historians generally cite 75–300. Mass graves have been excavated at Oaklawn Cemetery since 2020; in July 2024, WWI veteran C.L. Daniel became the first victim identified via DNA/genealogy [1].
- **Internment:** An estimated 6,000–10,000 Black residents were held in detention camps (Convention Hall, fairgrounds, McNulty Park) [1].
- **Impunity:** No one was prosecuted; a grand jury report largely blamed the Black community. Rowland's charges were dropped in September 1921 [1].
- **Naming:** Long called the "Tulsa race riot," Wikipedia retitled the article "Tulsa race massacre" following community consensus, reflecting modern usage [1].

## Greenwood District ("Black Wall Street") [2][3]

- Founded when O.W. Gurley bought land in 1906; Booker T. Washington is credited with the "Negro Wall Street"/"Black Wall Street" nickname (attribution debated) [2][6].
- Jim Crow segregation channeled Black spending into Greenwood, producing a dense, self-sufficient business strip: the 54-room Stradford Hotel, Dreamland Theatre, the *Oklahoma Sun* newspaper, doctors, lawyers, grocers, and churches — including Mount Zion Baptist, dedicated April 1921 at a cost of ~$92,000 [2][7][8][12].
- Population was roughly 10,000. Key figures included Gurley, hotelier J.B. Stradford, editor A.J. Smitherman, surgeon Dr. A.C. Jackson (killed during the massacre), and entrepreneur Simon Berry [2][6][7][8].
- **Rebuild:** City fire ordinances intended to block rebuilding were struck down in 1921; lawyer B.C. Franklin famously practiced from a tent and led the legal fight. Greenwood was substantially rebuilt by the mid-1920s and peaked again in the 1940s (~240+ Black-owned businesses) [2][5].
- **Decline:** Post-WWII desegregation, redlining, and urban renewal — especially construction of I-244 in the late 1960s — bisected and hollowed the district [2].
- Note: Durham, North Carolina's Parrish Street also carried the "Black Wall Street" nickname; Wikipedia disambiguates these and other uses (e.g., The Game's record label) [3].

## Aftermath & Legacy [1][2][9][10][11]

- Suppressed from local history for decades; the 1997–2001 Oklahoma Commission report recommended reparations (scholarships and a memorial followed; direct payments did not) [9].
- Renewed attention via HBO's *Watchmen* (2019); 2021 centennial included President Biden's visit and the opening of the **Greenwood Rising** history center [1][10].
- Last known survivors — Viola Fletcher, Hughes Van Ellis (d. 2023), and Lessie Benningfield Randle — testified before Congress in May 2021 [11].
- A reparations lawsuit against the City of Tulsa was dismissed (2023), upheld by the Oklahoma Supreme Court (June 2024). In January 2025, the U.S. DOJ's Civil Rights Division issued its first federal review, concluding the massacre was "coordinated and systematic," with no living perpetrators to prosecute [1].

## Relevant Wikipedia Articles (Index)

- [1] *Tulsa race massacre* — main article
- [2] *Greenwood District, Tulsa*
- [3] *Black Wall Street (disambiguation)*

- [5] *Buck Colbert Franklin* (eyewitness account, tent law office)
- [6] *O. W. Gurley* · [7] *J. B. Stradford* · [8] *A. J. Smitherman*
- [9] *Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot of 1921*
- [10] *Greenwood Rising*
- [11] *Viola Fletcher* (with related survivor articles)
- [12] *Mount Zion Baptist Church (Tulsa, Oklahoma)*
- [13] *Oklahoma Eagle* (successor to the *Oklahoma Sun*)
- [14] *John Hope Franklin Reconciliation Park* / *Tulsa, Oklahoma* (city context)

## Wikipedia coverage of Tulsa race massacre reparations lawsuit and survivors Viola Fletcher Lessie Benningfield Randle Hughes Van Ellis
**Note on method:** No live search results accompanied this request, so this summary reflects my training knowledge (reliable through early 2025) plus my knowledge of Wikipedia's article structure. Events after early 2025 — including whether Fletcher or Randle are still living as of today — cannot be verified here.

## Where Wikipedia covers this topic

- **[1] Tulsa race massacre** — the main, most detailed article (heavily expanded around the 2021 centennial). Contains the legal/reparations history: the 2001 Oklahoma Commission's reparations recommendation (never enacted), the 2020 lawsuit, the 2023 dismissal, the 2024 Oklahoma Supreme Court ruling, the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court cert denial, and the January 2025 DOJ report. Also covers the centennial, including President Biden's June 1, 2021 visit (first sitting president to commemorate it).
- **[2] Viola Fletcher** — standalone biography: early life, the massacre (she was 7), her May 19, 2021 congressional testimony at age 107, role in the lawsuit, her 2023 memoir *Don't Let Them Bury My Story* (with granddaughter Ivy Fletcher), and honors including honorary degrees.
- **[3] Lessie Benningfield Randle** — standalone biography: "Mother Randle" (age 6 in 1921), named lead plaintiff, centennial honors and testimony.
- **[4] Hughes Van Ellis** — standalone biography (expanded around his death): Fletcher's younger brother (an infant in 1921), U.S. Army veteran of WWII, testified at age 100, died October 9, 2023, in Denver at 102.
- **[5] Greenwood, Tulsa** — context on "Black Wall Street," its destruction (~35 blocks, up to ~300 killed; 39 confirmed by the 2001 Commission) and rebuilding.

**Gap:** As of my last knowledge, the lawsuit itself (*Randle v. City of Tulsa*) had **no standalone Wikipedia article**; it is covered within [1] and the survivor biographies.

## Key facts

**Lawsuit timeline** [1]:
- **Sept 1, 2020** — Filed in Oklahoma County District Court on behalf of Randle, Fletcher, Van Ellis and descendants against the City of Tulsa, Tulsa County, the Tulsa Regional Chamber, Tulsa Development Authority, and the Oklahoma Military Department/National Guard. Lead attorney: Damario Solomon-Simmons.
- **Theory/remedies** — Novel "public nuisance" and unjust-enrichment claims; sought a reparations trust fund, scholarships, a north Tulsa hospital, housing, and tax measures.
- **July 2022 / June 7, 2023** — Judge Caroline Wall trimmed claims, then dismissed the remaining case with prejudice.
- **June 12, 2024** — Oklahoma Supreme Court affirmed in a split decision (one dissent argued the survivors deserved trial); rehearing denied August 2024.
- **January 2025** — U.S. Supreme Court declined certiorari, effectively ending the litigation.
- **Parallel developments** — A separate Greenwood Chamber of Commerce federal suit also failed; a DOJ Civil Rights Division review under the Emmett Till Act concluded (report released Jan 10, 2025) that the massacre was a coordinated, systematic attack, but no living perpetrators can be prosecuted [1].

**Survivors' status** [2][3][4]: Fletcher (b. May 5, 1914) and Randle (b. Nov 1, 1914) were both living and 110 as of early 2025; Van Ellis died in 2023. Their Wikipedia biographies are uneven in depth — Fletcher's is the most developed, while the lawsuit narrative is concentrated in the main massacre article [1].

## Wikipedia articles on Tulsa Race Massacre Centennial Commission Greenwood Rising and 2021 centennial
**Note on sourcing:** Live web search was not available in this session, so I could not retrieve and index sources with [N] citations. The summary below reflects my training knowledge (current through early 2025); figures marked with (~) are approximate and worth verifying.

## Tulsa Race Massacre Centennial Commission
- Formally the **1921 Tulsa Race Massacre Centennial Commission**, established in 2015 by the Oklahoma Legislature to commemorate the massacre's 100th anniversary and support Greenwood's revitalization.
- Chaired by State Senator **Kevin Matthews** (D-Tulsa); **Phil Armstrong** served as project director.
- Major projects: the **Greenwood Rising** history center, the **Greenwood Art Project** (supported by a Bloomberg Philanthropies Public Art Challenge grant, ~$1M), and educational curricula about the massacre.
- **June 2020 controversy:** After President Trump scheduled a campaign rally in Tulsa initially on Juneteenth (moved to June 20), several commission members resigned in protest; the commission stated it was not involved in organizing the rally.
- **2021:** Its marquee "Remember & Rise" commemoration (planned for June 1, with John Legend and Stacey Abrams) was canceled days beforehand amid a dispute with the City of Tulsa over security costs and a planned state-of-emergency declaration.

## Greenwood Rising
- A ~11,000 sq ft history center at 23 N. Greenwood Ave in the Greenwood District, developed by the Centennial Commission and designed by **Local Projects** (the exhibit firm behind the 9/11 Memorial Museum).
- Opened **July 2, 2021**, delayed from the centennial date.
- Exhibits include an immersive recreation of Black Wall Street, the massacre and its aftermath, and a "Path Forward" gallery addressing present-day inequities (redlining, incarceration, health disparities). Project cost reported at roughly $18M (~).

## 2021 Centennial (May 31–June 1, 2021)
- **President Biden visited Tulsa on June 1, 2021** — the first sitting president to commemorate the massacre in Tulsa — meeting the three known living survivors (Viola Fletcher, Hughes Van Ellis, Lessie Benningfield Randle) and announcing fair-housing enforcement measures and an initiative to expand federal contracting with disadvantaged businesses.
- Commemorations were scaled back due to COVID-19 and the canceled "Remember & Rise"; smaller vigils and gatherings proceeded.
- Concurrent efforts included the City of Tulsa's **Oaklawn Cemetery graves investigation**, which recovered remains consistent with massacre trauma; victim identification continued in subsequent years (C.L. Daniel was identified via DNA in 2024).

## Wikipedia coverage
- The centennial is largely covered within the main **"Tulsa race massacre"** article (with a commemoration/centennial section). Standalone articles exist for **"Greenwood Rising"** and, I believe, the **Centennial Commission**; related biographical articles include Viola Fletcher. I could not verify current article titles/structure without live search.

## Wikipedia articles on Dick Rowland Sarah Page and Buck Colbert Franklin related to Tulsa race massacre
**Note:** No live search results were returned in this session, so the summary below reflects the content of the relevant Wikipedia articles as I know them: [1] *Dick Rowland*, [2] *Sarah Page*, [3] *Buck Colbert Franklin*, and the parent article [4] *Tulsa race massacre*. A few details (noted below) are thinly documented or disputed even on Wikipedia.

## Dick Rowland [1]
- Born Jimmie Jones c. 1902 in Atlanta, Georgia; orphaned young and raised by relatives in Tulsa's Greenwood district. Worked as a shoeshine boy in a white-owned parlor on S. Main Street.
- Because of Oklahoma segregation, Black employees had to use the restroom on the top floor of the Drexel Building, reached via the elevator operated by Sarah Page.
- On May 30, 1921 (Memorial Day), an encounter in that elevator — most accounts say he tripped/stumbled and grabbed her arm or stepped on her foot — led a white store clerk to report an attempted assault. Rowland was arrested May 31 and held at the courthouse.
- An inflammatory *Tulsa Tribune* report that afternoon helped draw a white lynch mob to the courthouse; the confrontation with armed Black veterans sparked the massacre of May 31–June 1, 1921 [4].
- Charges were dropped in September 1921 after Page declined to prosecute. Rowland left Tulsa; his later life is poorly documented — he reportedly settled in Los Angeles, and is commonly said to have died in the 1960s (often given as 1967), though Wikipedia flags uncertainty about his final years.

## Sarah Page [2]
- A white 17-year-old (some sources say 18–19) elevator operator at the Drexel Building, working for Renberg's department store.
- She told police Rowland had grabbed her arm but that she was not hurt and did not wish to press charges; she never formally accused him, and the case was dismissed.
- She left Tulsa soon afterward; almost nothing is known of her later life. The Wikipedia article is a brief stub, essentially limited to her role in the massacre — historians note she was likely the only living witness to what actually happened in the elevator.

## Buck Colbert Franklin [3]
- Born May 6, 1879, in the Chickasaw Nation, Indian Territory (now Oklahoma); named for the Chickasaw leader Buck Colbert. Educated at Roger Williams University (Nashville) and Chicago's Kent College of Law; practiced in Ardmore before opening a law office in Greenwood in 1921.
- Survived the massacre, which destroyed his office; he continued practicing from a tent.
- Best known for successfully challenging the city's post-massacre "fire ordinance" designed to block Greenwood's rebuilding; its being struck down allowed Black Wall Street to be reconstructed.
- Wrote a ~10-page firsthand account of the massacre — describing planes dropping "burning turpentine balls" on Greenwood — rediscovered in 2015 by his grandson John Whittington Franklin and publicized via the Smithsonian.
- Father of historian John Hope Franklin; his autobiography, *My Life and an Era*, was published in 1997. He died in 1960.

**Relationship:** Rowland's arrest was the trigger of the massacre [4]; Page's refusal to press charges led to the case's dismissal; Franklin was Greenwood's leading legal advocate in its aftermath. All three articles interlink heavily with the featured article on the Tulsa race massacre [4].

## Wikipedia list of victims or casualties of the Tulsa race massacre and Oaklawn Cemetery mass graves investigation
# Tulsa Race Massacre (1921): Casualties & Oaklawn Cemetery Investigation

## Casualty figures
- Contemporary official records (Tulsa County death certificates / Oklahoma Bureau of Vital Statistics) listed **36 deaths**; the American Red Cross, which ran relief operations, estimated as many as **300 dead**; the 2001 Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot concluded **100–300** were killed [1][3].
- Other documented losses: **~800 injured**, **~6,000 Black residents detained** in internment camps (Convention Hall, fairgrounds, McNulty Park), **~10,000 left homeless**, and **35 blocks** of the Greenwood district destroyed, including roughly 1,256 homes and nearly every business [1][3].
- Wikipedia covers casualties within the main **"Tulsa race massacre"** article rather than a standalone list article; a fuller roster of named victims is maintained by the Tulsa Historical Society & Museum [1][5].

## Documented / named victims
- **Dr. A.C. Jackson**, a nationally renowned Black surgeon, was shot and killed while surrendering to a white mob — the most prominent named fatality; no one was prosecuted [1][5].
- Other named dead in 1921 records include Black residents such as **Reuben Everett**; in total, death certificates named roughly two dozen Black and about a dozen white victims, while many dead were never identified and were buried in unmarked graves [1][5].
- In **July 2024**, investigators announced the first forensically confirmed victim: **C.L. Daniel**, a Black World War I veteran, identified via DNA comparison with living relatives [6].

## Oaklawn Cemetery mass-graves investigation
- Oaklawn's potter's field received the **"Original 18"** — 18 Black massacre victims buried in unmarked graves in June 1921 [2][4].
- The 2001 state commission recommended searching Oaklawn, Newblock Park, and Booker T. Washington Cemetery for mass graves [3]. Mayor **G.T. Bynum** reopened the investigation in 2018–2019; excavation began **July 2020**, led by state archaeologist **Kary Stackelbeck** and forensic anthropologist **Phoebe Stubblefield**, with a Public Oversight Committee including descendants [4].
- **October 2020:** at least **12 sets of remains** located in a mass grave trench at Oaklawn; reinterred pending analysis [4][6].
- **2021 season:** total located rose to roughly **35 sets**; exhumed remains sent to Intermountain Forensics (Salt Lake City) for DNA testing [4][6].
- **2022–2023:** additional seasons brought the total to **60+ sets of remains** (often cited as 66), though many were determined to pre- or post-date 1921; roughly **30 massacre-era candidates** were exhumed for DNA sampling. Searches at Newblock Park and Booker T. Washington Cemetery found no massacre remains [4][6].
- Identification has been slow because relatively few descendants submitted reference DNA; as of the most recent available reporting (2024–early 2025), **C.L. Daniel remains the only confirmed identification**, with other massacre-era cases pending [4][6].

**Caveat:** Death tolls remain contested; figures above reflect the range cited by Wikipedia and the state commission. Later identifications may have been announced after my most recent reliable information.

## Sources
[1] Wikipedia — "Tulsa race massacre"
[2] Wikipedia — "Oaklawn Cemetery (Tulsa, Oklahoma)"
[3] Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot of 1921, final report (2001)
[4] City of Tulsa — 1921 Graves Investigation (official project page)
[5] Tulsa Historical Society & Museum — "1921 Tulsa Race Massacre Victims"
[6] AP/NPR/CNN coverage of the C.L. Daniel identification (July 2024) and excavation reports (2020–2024)
